sources.title: Martin R. Bridson and Andre Haefliger, Metric Spaces of Non-Positive Curvature (Springer Grundlehren 319, 1999; author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: Chapter I.5, SS5.6-5.10, printed pp. 59-62 (K-cones, the metric formula with the angular truncation theta=min{pi,d}, the cone on S^n, the metric-space proof, and the characterisation of geodesics); Chapter I.5, SS5.13-5.16, printed pp. 63-64 (spherical joins, the product-cone isometry and S^n*S^m = S^{n+m+1}); Chapter I.7, SS7.14-7.16, printed pp. 102-104 (links of points in geodesic simplices and in M_k-simplicial complexes, the intrinsic pseudometric with the value infinity between components, and cone neighbourhoods). Sections I.7.2-I.7.13 and I.7.17-I.7.19 were read by the sibling batch-6 reader for the preceding pair and are not re-read here; the page consumes their content only through that pair's items.

contents.name: I.5.6-I.5.7 Definition of the K-cone, the metric formula d(x,x')^2=t^2+t'^2-2tt'cos(min{pi,d(y,y')}), the recovery of the link metric from the cone, and the through-the-apex geodesics when d(y,y')>=pi
I.5.8 The cone over S^n is isometric to Euclidean space E^{n+1} (and to a hemisphere for K>0)
I.5.9(1) The cone formulae define a metric: the triangle inequality by a case analysis on the sum of the two adjacent angular distances
I.5.9(2) The cone over Y is complete if and only if Y is complete
contents.reason: No item of this pair asserts or consumes completeness of a cone; the local product chart uses only the local metric, length and geodesic structure of the cone over a link, and global completeness of cones belongs to a later curvature development if needed.

contents.name: I.5.10 Characterisation of geodesics in the cone: development of geodesics of the link when d(y1,y2)<pi, through-the-apex geodesics otherwise, and containment in the closed ball of radius max{t1,t2}
I.5.13-I.5.14 Definition of the spherical join, its cosine metric formula and the endpoint identifications
I.5.15-I.5.16 The natural isometry C_0(Y1*Y2) = C_0Y1 x C_0Y2 (from which the join metric is read off) and the corollary S^n*S^m = S^{n+m+1}
I.7.14 The link of a point in a geodesic simplex: unit vectors at x pointing into the simplex, and the small neighbourhood of x isometric to the cone ball over the link

I.7.15 The link Lk(x,K) of a point in an M_k-simplicial complex: equivalence classes of segments, the intrinsic pseudometric assembled from the links of the simplices containing x, and the value infinity when no string connects
I.7.16 Theorem: if the injectivity radius e(x) is positive then B(x,e(x)/2) is naturally isometric to the open ball of the same radius about the cone point of C_K(Lk(x,K))
I.7.17-I.7.18 The development of an m-string and radial projection
contents.reason: The taut-string development is an alternative route to the geodesic-existence theorem I.7.19 of the preceding pair; this page constructs its geodesics by the proper-target Ascoli argument and the planar sector development of a cone, so no item here consumes m-string developments.

sources.title: Michael W. Davis, The Geometry and Topology of Coxeter Groups (first-edition author manuscript, 2007-2008)
sources.locator: Appendix I.2, printed pp. 505-507 (the cone on a CAT(1)-space, the truncated angular distance theta(x,y)=min{pi,d(x,y)}, Proposition I.2.17, Lemmas I.2.18 and I.2.19, and the spherical join with its cosine metric); Appendix I.3, printed pp. 507-510 (X_k-cell structures, the geometric link Lk(F,P)=Cone(F,P) intersect S(E(F,P)), the link Lk(x,P) of a point, the facial identification Lk(x,Sigma) = S^{dim F-1}*Lk(F,Sigma) in the proof of Theorem I.3.5, and Lemma I.3.6 on local geodesics); Appendix A.4, printed pp. 412-414 (the join of convex polytopes and of abstract simplicial complexes, cells of the join, and Lemma A.4.7); Chapter 7, SS7.1, printed pp. 123-125 (Definition 7.1.1 and Examples 7.1.2-7.1.7: the nerve as the complex of spherical subsets).

contents.name: Appendix I.2 The cone Cone(X) over a metric space and the metric d_kappa with the truncated angle theta(x,y)=min{pi,d(x,y)}
Proposition I.2.17: if X is complete and pairs at distance <= pi are joined by geodesics then Cone_kappa(X) is a complete geodesic space; and Cone_kappa(X) is CAT(kappa) if and only if X is CAT(1)
Lemma I.2.18: Cone_0(X1) x Cone_0(X2) is isometric to Cone_0(X1*X2) with the product metric
Lemma I.2.19: the spherical join X1*X2 is CAT(1) if and only if both factors are CAT(1)
contents.reason: Curvature of joins is CAT(1) comparison material; this pair defines and measures the join but makes no curvature assertion, and the CAT page owns the cone/CAT equivalence.

contents.name: Appendix I.3 Definition I.3.1 and the geometric link Lk(F,P):=Cone(F,P) intersect S(E(F,P)), with Lk(x,P) the union of the links of the cells containing x, piecewise spherical
Theorem I.3.5 (the link condition) with its facial identification in the proof: for x in the relative interior of a cell F, Lk(x,Sigma) is isometric to the spherical join S^{dim F-1}*Lk(F,Sigma)
Theorem I.3.5 (statements (a)-(e)): an X_k-polyhedral complex has curvature <= kappa if and only if its links are CAT(1), with vertex and cell tests and the systole criterion
contents.reason: The link criterion is the CAT page's central theorem; this pair supplies only the angular link and cone vocabulary that the criterion consumes.

contents.name: Lemma I.3.6: a piecewise geodesic is a local geodesic at x0 if and only if the distance from c'_out to c'_in in Lk(x0,Sigma) is at least pi
contents.reason: Local geodesics and their link characterisation are part of the CAT/local-geodesic development of the later page, not of this metric-construction pair.

contents.name: Appendix A.4 The join of convex polytopes and of abstract simplicial complexes: cells of the join are joins of cells, the join with a point is the cone, and Lemma A.4.7 that joins of flag complexes are flag

SS7.1 Definition 7.1.1 and Examples 7.1.2-7.1.7: the nerve L(W,S) as the complex of spherical subsets; the universal Coxeter system has only the empty and singleton spherical subsets, so its nerve is a discrete set of vertices
